terms.comment: Tongs, pincers, forceps: the smith’s tongs (Verg. G. 4.175) and the surgeon’s (Lewis & Short). The clearest ancient word for a tool that grips.

evidence: M-O s.v. pliers / pincers, citing Kirsch and Helfer
terms.comment: Neo-Latin; not in Lewis & Short. It is not presented as ancient Latin.

terms.gloss: shears, scissors; in Celsus, a gripping forceps
terms.comment: Usually shears or scissors (Lewis & Short), and Servius draws the line: forficēs sunt quibus incīdimus, forcipēs quibus aliquid firmum tenēmus (on Verg. A. 8.453, quoted by Lewis & Short). But Celsus, as Marx prints him, pulls teeth with a forfex, and has a special one for roots, which he says has a Greek name (7.12.1). Lewis & Short cites the same chapter under forceps, after editions that read forcipe: the two words were confused by copyists, and Vitruvius 10.2 has both readings. So forfex for a gripping tool has ancient warrant, but forceps is the unambiguous word.
evidence: Cels. 7.12.1: tum, sī fierī potest, manū; sī minus, forfice, dēns excipiendus est
